models.collectorNote: Pre-war fours with known history are museum-tier. The DV-32 cars are among the most valuable American classics; engine-and-chassis number matching is the market.

generations.name: Bearcat (four-cylinder)
generations.note: Early cars used a Wisconsin T-head four of 389 cu in; later Bearcats used Stutz's own sixteen-valve four. Either way the recipe was the same: maximum engine, minimum car.

generations.name: Bearcat DV-32
generations.note: The Depression-era revival: a double-overhead-cam, 32-valve straight-eight under a cut-down speedster body. A supercharged DV-32 engine option was quoted at over 180 hp; very few Bearcats of either kind were built in the thirties.

models.intro: The brass-age sports car in its purest form: two bucket seats, a fuel tank, a huge four-cylinder engine and nothing else. The Bearcat made Stutz's name at Indianapolis in 1911, 'the car that made good in a day', and the name returned on the supercharged DV-32 cars of the thirties.

models.collectorNote: Weymann fabric bodies are the fragile treasure, original fabric is nearly irreplaceable. DV-32-powered cars command the DV premium.

generations.name: Series AA–M / Blackhawk
generations.note: The 1926 Series AA's 287 cu in eight made 92 hp; the line grew through the BB and M series to the DV-32 cars. A Stutz Blackhawk held the 24-hour speed record in 1928, averaging over 106 mph at Daytona.

models.intro: Stutz reinvented itself as a luxury marque: the Vertical Eight brought an overhead-cam straight-eight, hydraulic brakes and safety glass to a company built on speed, and the Weymann fabric-body cars gave it Parisian style. The Blackhawk speed records of 1928 were the proof of speed.
